newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Psychiatrist links Argentine tycoon to murder.
newsitem.headline: Psychiatrist links Argentine tycoon to murder.

text.p: A man accused of killing Argentine photographer Jose Luis Cabezas confessed to a police psychiatrist he had been told to "lean on" the newsman by tycoon Alfredo Yabran, the psychiatrist testified on Tuesday.

"To lean on him, give Mr. Cabezas a fright, not to kill him. That's what was agreed and discussed with Mr. Yabran," the defendant, former police inspector Gustavo Prellezo, said, according to a statement read by psychiatrist Jose Abasolo in court.
Lawyer Jorge Diez -- defending another man accused of taking part in the crime -- read the testimony to Reuters. The declaration was also read on local television.

The psychiatrist said Prellezo told him that he and a gang of former police and petty criminals kidnapped and accidentally killed Cabezas after he met Yabran twice. Prellezo did not say why Yabran wanted to scare Cabezas.

Yabran, a postal tycoon who is suing former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo for accusing him of being a "mafia" boss, denies any involvement in the killing and has paid for advertisements in national newspapers complaining of persecution.

Yabran has not been charged in the case and said his accusers were trying to further their political careers or remove him from competition in upcoming privitizations of the state post office and the airports.

Cabezas, a 35-year-old father of two who worked for weekly news magazine Noticias, was abducted at a beach resort in January, beaten, shot in the head and doused with fuel. His charred corpse, found inside his burned-out car, was identifiable only by his watch.
Prellezo, who has been accused by other suspects of killing Cabezas, said one of his accomplices shot him accidentally after roughing him up.
Prellezo's lawyer told reporters he was shocked that a psychiatrist should reveal what was discussed with a patient.
"This should have come under some sort of professional secret. Otherwise they should tell those being held that their every word can be used against them," Hector Mestre said.
Prellezo has declined to testify since he was arrested in April, but was made to undergo sessions with the police psychiatrist.
Cabezas made a name in journalism by taking a rare photo of camera-shy Yabran walking on a beach with his wife, which the newspaper Noticias ran on its cover.

His killing brought back memories of thousands of similarly brutal murders under Argentina's military juntas in the 1970s. Huge crowds took to the streets to demand justice for the photographer and the journalists' union covered Buenos Aires with posters reading, "Don't forget Cabezas."

The investigation has taken on political significance in Argentina and Buenos Aires Gov. Eduardo Duhalde, one of the leading candidates for presidential elections in 1999, has staked much political capital on the culprits being caught.
The silver-haired, burly Yabran and his security chief Gregorio Rios have been questioned as witnesses over phone calls Prellezo made to Yabran's home in the days before Cabezas was murdered.
Yabran said in his ad that he was "one of the people most eager" to have the case solved "without subordination to commercial interests or premeditated political campaigns."
